articles.title: Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally
articles.summary: Cockroach Janta Party standoff with government extended as youth-led movement calls protest over jailing of activists.
articles.body:
Authorities have tightened security in New Delhi after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called for a new protest over the jailing of two of its activists .

Thousands of additional police officers were deployed in the Indian capital on Friday as the Indian government appeared to prepare for further confrontations. The youth-led CJP movement has held a series of protests in recent weeks to demand India’s election chief resign . Its demonstrations have been met with a tough crackdown.

CJP supporters have been called to gather in New Delhi’s Central Park at 5pm (11:30am GMT). The rally was called after two of the movement’s leaders were jailed for five days this week for allegedly trespassing at a protest site.

Authorities have closed the park, citing “administrative reasons”, and set up metal barricades at key intersections.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke suggested police may try to arrest him before the protest but declared he and his supporters are “not afraid” and are “ready” to go to jail.

In a social media post, Dipke accused the government of hypocrisy and denounced police crackdowns against the movement.

Members of the government may never have come to power had they experienced similar protest restrictions, he asserted.

“The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition,” Dipke said.

“Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are.”

The rally is just the latest facing a crackdown by the authorities.

The CJP has held almost daily demonstrations this month demanding electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The commissioner oversaw the removal of more than 130 million names from the electoral roll and is accused by the CJP of voter fraud. Election authorities said the changes were made to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

The CJP was founded in May amid anger over the leaking of exam papers and the poor prospects facing India’s youth.

The movement swiftly became a conduit for India’s Gen Z, many of whom feel disenfranchised during an unemployment crisis under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s right-wing government. The movement has since forced the resignation of the education minister.

With the political opposition quick to support the protests, Modi has come under intense pressure with some analysts saying he is now facing the worst crisis since he came to office in 2014.

articles.title: Zelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates
articles.summary: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky praised “real leaders” in Europe at a summit in Belgium on Friday, taking a veiled swipe at US President Donald Trump amid testy relations between Kyiv and Washington.
articles.body: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky praised “real leaders” in Europe at a summit in Belgium on Friday, taking a veiled swipe at US President Donald Trump amid testy relations between Kyiv and Washington. European leaders are rallying around Zelensky after the White House heaped pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, even as Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continue unabated. After halting strikes on Russian oil refineries for three days at the request of the United States, Ukraine has resumed those attacks given Russia didn’t adhere to US President Donald Trump’s so-called “energy ceasefire.” Trump, who is desperate for soaring global diesel prices to ease ahead of next month’s midterm elections, blindsided European leaders last week when he struck a deal allowing Russian diesel exports, a move Zelensky said had left him feeling betrayed. The US president has blamed the rise in fuel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, eager to deflect attention from his war in Iran which remains deeply unpopular with voters. On Thursday, Trump once again lashed out at Zelensky in an interview with Newsmax, calling him “not a good guy for us to deal with.” “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country,” Trump said, without acknowledging Russia’s invasion. “I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.” As Zelensky arrived at Friday’s summit in Brussels, flanked by the European Union’s top leaders, he didn’t mention the deterioration in US relations, but was keen to emphasize the strength of his relationship with the EU. “I’m so thankful that we have such huge support from (the) EU Council, Commission and leaders – real leaders – so that they stay with us from the very beginning of this war,” Zelensky said as he walked into the summit. “Of course we want to end this war as quick as possible. We don’t see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this,” the Ukrainian president said, adding that “energy needs” were at the top of his agenda ahead of the winter. Amid a challenging week diplomatically, Ukraine has also run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday. “It’s an open secret that we are not a priority destination for these missiles now,” Zelensky told a news conference on Friday, noting that most Patriot interceptors were now being sent to the Middle East. But he added that Ukraine was grateful to the Europeans “who are financing all of this,” as well as to NATO and to the White House. When a reporter asked whether he thought Trump was treating Ukraine as a scapegoat for his own problems given high fuel prices and the ongoing Iran war, Zelensky paused for a full 15 seconds. With a smile, he told the silent room: “This is my answer.” Earlier the Ukrainian president said his team was in constant contact with US negotiators and would arrange a meeting in the coming days. “We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added. “When the quality of life is so terrible during wartime, maintaining dignity is a very important thing.” EU leaders said they were preparing a new package of sanctions against Russia – the 22nd package since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In contrast with the Trump administration, they were keen to stress that sanctions against Moscow would be strengthened unless Putin stops the war. “We supported President Trump’s energy ceasefire, but we’ve seen that Russia did not respect it – not a single minute. Instead, Russia escalated, and therefore we have to increase the pressure on Russia,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. Zelensky has urged EU leaders to step up financial and military support for Ukraine, which urgently needs more air defenses to protect civilian and energy infrastructure from relentless Russian strikes. CNN’s Victoria Butenko and Daria Tarasova-Markina contributed to this report.

articles.title: Texas woman sentenced to 7 years in prison, annual jail time during probation for deadly DUI crash
articles.summary: Lynlee Pollis, who was sentenced to prison in a deadly DUI crash, must return to jail for 15 days each year on dates tied to the victims' birthdays and the anniversary of 2023 crash in Dallas.
articles.body: A Texas woman convicted of killing a college student in a drunken-driving crash was sentenced to seven years in prison and ordered to return to jail for 15 days each year while on probation. Lynlee Pollis, 30, was sentenced Wednesday after being convicted of intoxication manslaughter and intoxication assault in the September 2023 crash that killed 19-year-old Southern Methodist University student Honor Wallace and seriously injured her friend, Catherine "CeCe" Solberg, according to The Dallas Morning News. State District Judge Jennifer Balido also ordered Pollis to serve 10 years of probation following her release from prison, including 15 days in jail annually. Some of the required jail dates coincide with the victims' birthdays, Pollis' birthday and the anniversary of the deadly crash, according to the newspaper. NEVADA PAROLE BOARD REJECTS HENRY RUGGS III'S BID FOR EARLY RELEASE AFTER DEADLY 156 MPH DUI CRASH The sentence came after roughly three hours of jury deliberations following a two-and-a-half-week trial. During the trial, Solberg's father, Bobby Solberg, delivered an emotional victim impact statement criticizing Pollis for putting the families through the lengthy proceedings. "You were so drunk, and you wouldn’t admit it. You made us sit through this [trial] for three weeks," Solberg said. "We’ve seen no personal accountability from you." PROMINENT BUSINESSMAN LEARNS FATE IN BOAT CRASH CASE THAT KILLED TEEN, MAIMED ANOTHER Wallace's father, David Wallace, also confronted Pollis in his victim impact statement. "You took the most precious gift from us through your selfishness," he said. "Own it. Own what you did." On Sept. 24, 2023, Wallace was driving her Volkswagen Jetta through a green light in Dallas when Pollis' Lexus SUV slammed into her vehicle. Wallace was pronounced dead at the hospital, while Solberg, a passenger in the Jetta, suffered a shoulder injury and concussion. She was later diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury, according to The Dallas Morning News. DRUNK REPEAT OFFENDER CALLED A 'TICKING TIME-BOMB' BEFORE 80-MPH BOATING COLLISION KILLED WOMAN: PROSECUTORS According to testimony from prosecution experts cited by the newspaper, Pollis was traveling approximately 67 mph in a 35-mph zone and drove through a traffic light that had been red for at least five seconds. Pollis' husky named Tequila, who was also in the vehicle, was not hurt. The newspaper reported that testing showed Pollis had a blood alcohol concentration of 0.294%, nearly four times Texas' legal limit of 0.08%. According to the initial arrest affidavit, officers noticed Pollis had glassy eyes, slurred speech and an odor of alcohol when they interviewed her at the hospital. Her attorneys had sought probation rather than prison, pointing to her lack of prior felony convictions. articles.title: Japan’s Takaichi says chores and makeup add hours to her workday, sparking debate on gender roles
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi‘s comments about the additional work she has to take on as a woman compared with her male predecessors have sparked a debate about gender roles in the country and have put her performance under the spotlight.
articles.body: TOKYO — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comments about the additional work she has to take on as a woman compared with her male predecessors have sparked a debate about gender roles in the country and have put her performance under the spotlight. On Wednesday, Takaichi said she works longer hours than her male predecessors because she needs to fulfill requirements for women, such as house chores and applying makeup. “In the morning, I take a bath, fix breakfast and do the dishes, then apply makeup,” Takaichi told a parliamentary session Wednesday. “Doing these things, I feel I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers.” It took a while for her aides to learn that she needs extra time to fix her makeup and be more presentable before going on camera, Takaichi said. Her emphasis on makeup, bathing and house chores quickly backfired, because she was seen as promoting old-fashioned gender roles and excessive working hours that have long been considered problems in Japan. In a country where gender roles remain rigid and long hours at work are the norm for men, working women are also burdened with house chores and child care. Women spend nearly five hours doing house chores daily, compared with about 40 minutes spent by an average male, the latest government figures show. Comments on social media noted that many working women in Japan who raise children or take care of elderly parents face even heavier demands than Takaichi, saying that her comment is a matter of time management and her outdated view on gender equality. “As long as she gets her job done, it’s fine if she needs more time than men ... but seeking forgiveness because she needs time to put on makeup as an excuse is unacceptable,” Fusako Miwa, a lawyer, said on social media. Takaichi’s work mantra and her revelation of zero to three hours of sleep at night due to her homemaking burden on top of her heavy workload after taking office last year triggered criticism that she was setting the wrong example for work-life balance and gender equality. While Takaichi regularly comments on X, she has been scaling back on her appearances at parliament and has largely holed up at her residence at night and on weekends, a tendency criticized as neglect of policy debate. Takaichi also suffered a setback as her newly appointed farm minister, Kazuo Yana, resigned Wednesday over multiple scandals, including boasting about cutting the road construction budget for municipalities that did not support him in an election. Yana also admitted arranging questionable free transportation for his supporters at his political rallies. The prime minister’s time management was brought up by Fumitake Fujita, a top official of Takaichi’s junior coalition partner, Japan Innovation Party, on Wednesday when he suggested reducing hourslong parliamentary sessions that ministers need to attend almost daily. Japan’s prime minister attended parliamentary sessions for 72 days in 2022, compared with 50 in Britain and 13 in Germany, Fujita said, citing a recent report by political think tank NXJI Research. The report proposed introducing cooks and other housekeeping staff at the prime minister’s official residence so the leader can concentrate on official duties and get sufficient sleep. Takaichi said managing her busy schedule has been difficult, and she routinely brings home a thick stack of documents. “I do enjoy reading them late at night,” Takaichi said. “Honestly, I feel it is not easy to squeeze out time to sit down and think about the future direction of Japan or have a grand vision.”

articles.title: Land once reserved for New York's Shoreham nuclear plant has become Long Island's largest DEC acquisition, with the state paying $28.25 million to permanently protect nearly 750 coastal acres
articles.summary: A nuclear power project abandoned decades ago has left behind nearly 750 acres of undeveloped coastal land in New York.
articles.body: A nuclear power project abandoned decades ago has left behind nearly 750 acres of undeveloped coastal land in New York. The state has now purchased the property for $28.25 million to protect its forests, wetlands and shoreline permanently. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the acquisition on Thursday, marking the largest purchase of land on Long Island by the New York state department of environmental conservation (DEC), LongIsland.com reported.The property surrounds the former Shoreham nuclear power plant in Suffolk County. It stretches across parts of Shoreham and Wading river, along Long Island Sound. Although the nuclear facility was abandoned in 1989, much of the adjoining land remained undeveloped. The state will now manage the area for environmental conservation and eventually open designated sections to visitors.The purchase ends a conservation effort that had continued for more than a decade. Environmental groups had long sought protection for the site because of its coastal forests, rare plant species and importance to Long Island's groundwater supply. DEC identified the property for preservation in its 2016 conservation plan and included it again in the draft plan for 2026.The state acquired the land from National Grid using money from several environmental funding programmes.A failed nuclear projectThe Shoreham nuclear power project had become a major source of disagreement on Long Island. Residents raised concerns about safety and emergency arrangements, including how communities would be evacuated if a nuclear accident occurred.Therefore, the plant was built but never entered full commercial operation. The project was abandoned in 1989 following years of controversy, and the facility was decommissioned in 1994.After the project ended, the land surrounding the plant remained largely unused. Its future, however, continued to attract attention from environmental organisations that wanted the property protected and not developed.Richard Amper, a conservation campaigner associated with the Long Island Pine Barrens Society, was among those who supported its preservation. According to News 12 New York, Amper had proposed nearly a decade ago that the area should become a state park or join the Pine Barrens Preserve. His conservation work had contributed to protection of more than 100,000 acres on Long Island. Amper died in March this year, aged 81.Importance of Shoreham landProtecting Long Island's groundwater supply is one of the reasons environmental groups have supported the preservation of the Shoreham property. The island depends on a sole-source aquifer, an underground water source. Conservation groups say the forests and wetlands on the land can help replenish groundwater, reduce flooding and limit pollution entering nearby bays and Long Island Sound.The property is also important for wildlife. It provides habitats for several bird species, including osprey and the endangered piping plover. Rare native plants and other coastal species are also found in the area. Its preservation means these habitats will remain protected from future development.The nearly 750-acre property contains several different types of natural landscapes. Along the coast are sand and gravel beaches and bluffs rising to approximately 100 feet. Other parts of the land contain pine barrens, coastal oak-heath forests and maritime shrublands. More than 40 acres are covered by tidal marshes and shrub swamps.Apart from its environmental importance, the property also contains a site of cultural significance. John Turner, co-founder of the Long Island Pine Barrens Society, identified Split Rock, a large glacial boulder complex, as a place that held spiritual importance for several indigenous Native American tribes. The protected land also includes nearly a mile of natural shoreline.The $28.25 million fundingNew York has funded the purchase through a combination of environmental programmes. The funding included contributions from the US Environmental Protection Agency's Long Island Sound Partnership Program, the New York State Clean Water Infrastructure Act and the 1996 Clean Water, Clean Air Bond Act.The acquisition also forms part of the state's '30x30' initiative, under which New York aims to protect 30% of its lands and waters by 2030.Visitors will eventually be able to use marked trails and designated beach access areas. articles.title: India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
articles.summary: The SIR is disenfranchising marginalised communities and advancing the Hindu nationalist project.
articles.body:
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy.

The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal.

Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”.

The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement.

Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice.

The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion. The pattern is repeated in the National Capital Region, Delhi, where nearly one-third of the existing electorate was missing from the draft SIR roll. Studies flag especially high rates of exclusion in areas with large minority and migrant populations and among residents of informal and unauthorised settlements. The disproportionate exclusion of Muslims suggests an ideological alignment between the SIR’s ostensibly impersonal bureaucracy and the social and political programme of the Hindu right.

As a political and ideological instrument, the exercise has proved to be doubly potent. Through mass deletion of voters from targeted social categories, such as Muslims, it has contributed to shrinking the electoral base of the BJP’s principal rivals. The elections in Bihar and Bengal after the SIR suggest a discernible pattern. In the 2020 Bihar Assembly elections, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD)-led alliance lost to the BJP-led alliance by just 0.03 percentage points in vote share. In contrast, in the 2025 elections after the removal of 6.8 million names from the existing rolls and the addition of 2.1 million new voters, the BJP alliance’s lead increased to nearly 9 percentage points. Analysis of the 2026 Bengal Assembly elections also points to the decisive role SIR deletions played in the electoral outcome. The exercise disproportionately affected Muslim, migrant and poorer voters in districts where the BJP had historically struggled to gain support. In many constituencies won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the party’s margin of victory.

Furthermore, the bureaucratic exercise reinforces the larger ideological project of a “pure Hindu” nation. It has also legitimised calls for the expulsion of “Rohingyas”, “infiltrators” and “Bangladeshis”, terms used as dog whistles for Muslims, helping to polarise elections along communal lines. Although Bengali Hindus and others also found their names removed from electoral rolls, the political messaging around the SIR in a communally charged election campaign cast Muslims as a suspect community, imperilling their civil and social rights. Predictably, the newly elected BJP governments in Bihar and Bengal moved to deny Public Distribution System benefits to those who found their names expunged from the electoral rolls.

The SIR is thus fuelled by the imagined spectre of a vile and illicit intruder who must be expelled to preserve the existing order. It follows the Supreme Court-supervised National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam, which left 1.9 million of the state’s residents, mostly Bengali speakers, essentially stateless. It also resembles the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, which introduced religiously differentiated access to citizenship, an affront to the republic’s secular structure. The recently established High-Level Committee on Demographic Change, mandated to assess demographic changes occurring across India due to “illegal infiltration” and “abnormal” population changes among “religious and social communities”, is cut from the same cloth. Ultimately, the SIR is one of several instruments at play to criminalise, disenfranchise and denationalise social groups and communities considered inimical to the Hindutva vision of an ethnic state.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: He robbed the Van Gogh Museum. Now he wants to help secure the Louvre
articles.summary: One year after the Louvre heist, an ex-art thief sees weak spots all over: “If they asked me, I would show them that I can still get in.”
articles.body: Octave Durham has a question for the Louvre, a year after the revered French museum fell victim to what was dubbed the “heist of the century.” “Why don’t they approach me to do the security?” Durham is not a security specialist or even a trained guard, but a former art thief. Now “retired” from a life of crime, the 53-year-old describes himself on his Instagram account as the “Dutch Lupin,” inspired by the gentleman thief made famous by French star Omar Sy on Netflix. There’s no doubting Durham’s credentials. “I robbed banks, safety deposits, armored trucks. You name it, I robbed it,” he said in a phone interview. Then, in 2002, he and an accomplice broke into Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, making off with two paintings by the post-impressionist. Durham was later apprehended and served time in prison for the crime, but not before selling the paintings to a notorious crime boss who was later found in possession of the art. These days, Durham is still interested in stolen art –– but with the aim of doing good. He uses his underworld contacts to help recover some of these priceless artworks. Durham never gets paid, saying he does it mostly for “fun,” adding “it feels good to make people happy.” But suggest he is an informant and he immediately hits back. “I’m not an informant, I’m a contact. It’s a big difference. I don’t talk to police.” The person he does talk to is Arthur Brand, a Dutch self-styled detective known as the “Indiana Jones of the art world” who works alongside international police forces. According to Brand, Durham was key to the recovery of another stolen Van Gogh that made headlines in 2023. Taken from a Dutch museum in 2020, “Spring Garden” was later handed to Brand in a blue IKEA bag –– and he subsequently transferred it to the authorities. Brand has since helped recover a Pieter Brueghel masterpiece stolen in Poland in the 1970s and a painting looted from a Jewish family by the Nazi Hermann Göring, among other things. “I’ve had Picassos at my home and a ring of Oscar Wilde,” said Brand, who earns his living advising art collectors on prospective purchases. The detective work is a pro bono side hustle –– and one that appears likely to get busier. Just hours after the Louvre heist last October –– which saw thieves strike during broad daylight and make off with Napoleonic-era treasures –– another French museum was similarly targeted. This time, burglars stole gold and silver coins worth more than $100,000. Since then, attacks on museums, galleries and other cultural institutions have never been far from the headlines. Two Renoirs were stolen from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera last month (and found weeks later). Another Renoir, a Cézanne and a Matisse were taken from the Magnani Rocca Foundation near Parma, Italy, in March (and also later recovered), while four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina were seized from a Sicilian museum in August. That same month, criminals nabbed a $4 million diamond necklace from Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts (MAK). A recent report by the European Policing Agency (Europol) warned that museum thieves are becoming increasingly brazen, violent and aggressive. “Art theft has always been there,” said Brand. “I always say if art was invented on Monday, the first art was stolen on Tuesday and the first art was forged on Wednesday.” Nevertheless, he admits things have ramped up over the past year since the Louvre heist. “I talk to ex-thieves, and they hear from current thieves who say, ‘wow, the Louvre, let’s do it.’ They’re thinking: ‘If that’s possible, our local museum must be even more simple.’” When these heists happen, would-be art thieves are emboldened, Brand says. “Banks these days have less cash, jewelry shops are better secured, so they turn to museums. They’re vulnerable. It’s like a candy shop for thieves.” Europe’s weak spots While the problem is global, European galleries are particularly enticing for burglars, according to Brand. For one, much of the world’s commercially valuable art hails from there. And then there’s security. “Museums in Europe don’t have armed guards,” he said, adding that many are housed in historic buildings dating as far back as the 15th century. “It’s not Fort Knox.” Such “copycat” crimes following the Louvre heist are regarded as relatively risk-free, according to Ibrahim Balut, a museum security expert based in Belgium. “What we are seeing more and more of is smash and grab. Offenders aren’t scared anymore,” he said. “In Vienna, in the Renoir Museum and in the Louvre, they entered and left with the objects in less than three minutes. They come well prepared and attack in a short time.” Having recently visited the Louvre, Durham believes the world’s largest art museum is still vulnerable. “It has weak spots all over,” he said, adding that he spotted cracked windows. “They have secured the spot where they did the burglary. They put an iron fence over the entrance where they went in and a camera on the top. But what is the chance they will go back to the same spot? All the windows on the side are still the same.” The Louvre did not respond to a request for comment from CNN. The Europol report, meanwhile, revealed that these heists are increasingly using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars –– and even explosives. “Offenders are using more heavy material because everything is battery powered now,” explained Balut. “So they can use electrical equipment that are flexible, easier to handle, and they can attack quite fast.” It is the very nature of museums that makes them vulnerable, said Balut. “The mission and vision of a museum is to be open. It’s not like a bank or jewelry store where you cannot enter easily. In a museum it’s all open and the only thing holding you back from going immediately towards an object is a showcase or maybe a guard.” “Museums are investing more and more in security, but you have to understand that criminals are also getting more educated about things,” he added. “They have been to the museum to do a dry run, to see the items, what they can easily grab, how easy it is to flee.” Balut offers cultural institutions expert safety guidance, or, as he sees it: “I sell time. When criminals see that the reaction time of security and police is far faster, they will never do it again.” That involves a strategy that invests in people and not just cameras. “Security awareness must be at the forefront of everyone’s minds, not just the security staff but the museum directors, the curators, the restorers.” Finding a buyer The focus of art crime has also changed, according to Brand. “In the last 10 years, we’ve seen a shift to gold, silver, diamonds. You can melt them down or recut diamonds, leaving no evidence.” So why are priceless paintings still being targeted? “It’s stupidity,” said Brand. “They see that a painting by Van Gogh could be worth 50 million, so they think ‘well, it takes four minutes, let’s go and grab it.’ And then the problems start.” “They turn on the television the day after and find out that this painting is flagged in every database. Sometimes they think they’ll find a Dr. No, some villain who has this stash of stolen art. But they don’t exist.” Nevertheless, Brand admits some steal art as a kind of bargaining tool. “In the underworld, a stolen painting is worth 10% of what its value is on the market so it could be collateral,” he said. “Sometimes a mafia boss buys a stolen painting as insurance. Then one day, when he gets caught, he’ll say: ‘You want to give me 20 years for drugs, but I have a stolen Van Gogh. Let’s make a deal.’” A museum’s eyes and ears Another group of people with whom Brand is in regular contact is museum staff. “They’re panicking,” he said. “You must understand that people who work in museums, and it could be a curator or an expert or a museum director, they study art. They love art. It’s so out of their world, these crimes, and they don’t even want to think about it. So they are not prepared.” Lynda Albertson, head of the Association for Research into Crimes against Art, said criminals exploit a combination of factors: “Valuable, portable objects, in museums with identifiable security weaknesses, whose protection needs exceed their currently exercised security resources.” She said that while some museums are “doing a great deal” to improve security measures, others “have serious gaps.” “A camera can give you an excellent record of a theft without stopping it. Protection requires layers: current risk assessments, appropriate physical barriers and display cases, maintained alarms, trained staff, and a response that has actually been rehearsed,” said Albertson. Things like these matter “just as much as having someone watching a room or the entrance.” “Unfortunately, donors rarely queue up to put their names on an upgraded alarm system or to pay for additional guards, but those investments can determine whether a collection is targeted or not,” she said. As for Durham, he would happily give the Louvre some pointers, if given half a chance. “If they asked me, I would show them that I can still get in.”

articles.title: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
articles.summary: It is the first time the president has addressed nuclear weapons, but he didn’t deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition , nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.

In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.

“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.

The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.

He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.

“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.

He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.

Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.

“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”

Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.

Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.

Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.

When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.

The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.

It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.

“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”

However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.

What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?

Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.

Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.

In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.

He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.

Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.

Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.

“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.

Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.

The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.

What might another US attack on Iran look like?

With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.

The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.

Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.

Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.

Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

articles.title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland detained for UK murder plot
articles.summary: Johannes Natland, 19, travelled to West Yorkshire to carry out a "hit" in March last year.
articles.body:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."

Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.

When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed.

"There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan.

"We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."

Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.

Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school.

He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".

He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.

Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".

The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."

Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.

He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.

Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.

He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.

The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets.

"You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."

From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room.

At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die."

Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission."

According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it.

"I can kill someone and life will be wonderful."

Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified".

He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn't."

Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he would have shot himself in the foot to get out of the "pickle" he was in.

Flanagan said: "Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot Network, an organised criminal group sanctioned by the UK and the US due to its involvement in orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime.

"The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case.

"However, as recent events have shown, Counter Terrorism Policing will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK."

Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.

Counter Terrorism Policing said it continued to investigate those suspected of helping Natland obtain firearms and a stolen car.

In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and was later released under investigation.

Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods, specifically a car.

They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

articles.title: Compromises, bribes and a 400-year-old finger: The messy reality of getting my teenager to love Italy
articles.summary: On family trips to Italy, one mom is eager to show her son the country she fell in love with as an ex-pat. But their ideas of a great vacation don’t always align.
articles.body: One sparkling summer evening last year, I met up in Florence, Italy, with an Italian friend I hadn’t seen in years. After strolling through Piazza della Repubblica, Chiara and I lingered over novels at a bookstore and then had a long dinner at a lively restaurant near the central market. It was a thrill to catch up with a friend in the enchanting Tuscan city where we’d first met. My 13-year-old son, however, was with me, and after we said goodbye to my friend, he cut short my reverie. “That was three hours of hearing you talk, talk, talk Italian!” Leo yelled. He was tired, bored and angry. It was the same tone he’d used at the Uffizi, a world-class museum crammed full of Renaissance art. My husband and I had avoided taking him there before he was old enough to appreciate it, or so we thought. Our visit wound up being a mad dash past Botticelli paintings as Leo aimed to leave as swiftly as possible. On the way out, I craned my neck at all the art I wasn’t seeing. What’s more, when he’d learned that we were going to some cities from previous visits, he moaned, “What? Again? We’ve already been to Rome and Florence!” Ah, to be a jaded 13-year-old who’s not always aware of his privilege. What did impress him in Italy? Pokémon cards, a pricey Ferrari shirt and a touristy museum of illusions. He also enjoyed playing the card game Uno No Mercy, which we could have done at home. Oh, and the expensive café on the roof of the Uffizi? Yeah, that was good, too. It was Leo’s third trip to Italy and one of nearly 10 international trips already under his belt. We were visiting a country where I’d experienced a pivotal semester abroad, which led to a stint as an expat after studying Italian in college. None of that mattered. Either he was hot or bored or needed to use the bathroom. Or I’d overscheduled our day — something I loathe doing stateside. Traveling with children overseas is often challenging. My fierce attachment to Italy made it even harder. Why didn’t he love everything about the place that changed his mother’s life? But since I’m on a mission to convince Leo to fall for Italy, I’ve learned — mostly the hard way — to compromise. And despite some disagreements, my efforts have started to pay off. In fact, he makes the trips special — a thoroughly American boy who nonetheless shares a first name with Leonardo da Vinci and dreams of owning a Ferrari one day. Here’s what I’ve learned while traveling to Italy with my son. A funny thing happened on the way to the forum The afternoon we landed in Rome during our first family trip to Italy in 2018, I found myself renting a somewhat rickety quadricycle in the famed Villa Borghese park north of the city center, even though I was exhausted. Leo, who was five at the time, had spent our 10-hour flight squirming while draped across my lap. The heat that July day was stifling, and even though the park was near our hotel, it was hard to enjoy it because every minute there felt like standing by an open oven. The Villa Borghese is full of ancient marble statues, which Leo largely ignored. Already a keen admirer of Italian cars, he was much more interested in how fast we could round corners in the park while in the quadricycle, even if it meant nearly tipping over. He cackled with joy while steering this four-seat open-air vehicle that Italians call a rickshaw. The Roman Forum — and my nap — would have to wait, as would the excellent art museum that’s inside the park. The compromises continued during a return visit to Rome in 2022, when I found myself ransacking the city for Pokémon cards after an evening of al fresco dining started to wear on the patience of my fidgeting 10-year-old. One moment I was out with friends, the next dashing over to a bookshop. Italian novels are my passion, and I’d visited Mondadori, one of Italy’s largest booksellers, many times. But until that trip, I didn’t realize they stocked Pokémon cards. If I sound accommodating, while standing in line I fumed to myself, “This wasn’t what I wanted to show Leo in Italy.” When we finally went to the Roman Forum, I certainly hadn’t planned to cut short the visit because Leo needed to go to the bathroom and preferred to return to our lodgings. I managed to prolong our visit long enough to stick my head inside of the Temple of Venus but quickly had to throw in the towel. It was hot, he was tired and nothing could salvage the outing. But the scene was quite different at the museum in Florence that houses Galileo’s finger. The Italian astronomer died in 1642 so the finger is exactly as decrepit as you’d imagine, even through the museum’s protective glass case. But Leo, then aged 10, loved it. He was thrilled to learn admirers had severed the persecuted scientist’s middle finger when his remains were moved in the 1700s. If the finger felt like a gimmick, so did the overpriced drinks — in every city and at every stop. But that kept him entertained, as did his gaming console, which came in handy last year in Rome, when my husband and I slipped out to Piazza del Popolo for a glass of wine. I had qualms about leaving my son alone in an apartment in a foreign country — but Leo didn’t. The best Italian insults I also had qualms about what felt like millions of euros spent on tickets, half-eaten meals and a pair of sneakers that we hastily bought at the outlets near Florence because Leo had only packed Crocs. So I was eager for a cheap but meaningful outing, and I arranged a lunch with another Florentine friend. Cristiano has a one-liner for every occasion; during a previous trip back to Italy, he’d told me not to worry that I was losing my Italian skills by returning to live in America since I wasn’t making any new mistakes — just the same ones as before. Ba-dum-bum! He often likes to joke that his English isn’t very good because he had a bad teacher (me). When he asked if Leo knew Italian during our 2022 trip, I admitted only a little. “Leave it to me,” he said. At lunch in a piazza not far from the city’s Arno River, we ordered an antipasto and some primi before catching up. Then after asking for a piece of paper, Cristiano said, “How about that Italian lesson?” I handed him my travel diary so he could write his “lesson” directly into the notebook. As the two of them began chatting, I took a photo and beamed at my husband. A native speaker — and a dear friend — was giving our son a personalized Italian lesson! But I snapped to attention a moment later when I realized “cornuto” was the first word of the lesson. Strictly speaking, it isn’t a curse word — it simply means a cuckolded husband. Yet in a land where machismo still reigns, it’s considered a rather severe insult. When I looked at my notebook later, I saw Cristiano had drawn the accompanying hand symbol for cuckold — the pinkie and forefinger sticking out over the folded middle fingers — a universal symbol for bad luck in Italy. I’ve marveled endlessly over Italian but nothing really beats learning — at age 13 — the word to describe a man with a philandering wife. An Italian holiday for all Part of the challenge while traveling with children mirrors the general trickiness of parenting: what entertained a child when he was five may not work when he’s older. During our first trip to Italy as a family, Leo gushed over every monument. Our photos — of Leo smiling at the Vatican and posing at scenic overlooks — attest to that. At age five, he was simply happy to be with his parents while experiencing new sensations. But the boy we took to Italy the summer he turned 13 was no longer easily amused. The evening in Florence when we had dinner with my old friend, Chiara, I’d made sure some of the conversation was in English and there was food at the restaurant that he liked. But it didn’t matter. He’d learned that when I visit Italy, I’m totally seduced by Italian culture. His outburst following the dinner touched on the central tension. In Italy, I want to linger at the counter of every café I visit, and eavesdrop on a barista bantering in Italian with customers. I’m lost in a reunion with a world first encountered during the golden period of my life when I was a 20-something expat — the years against which all others are judged. Indeed, after three completed trips as a mom, I’ve now concluded the biggest compromise when I travel to Italy with Leo is accepting a holiday that’s much less about Italian cultural immersion, so that it’s one he can enjoy, too. That means passing up moments that are far more magical to me than to Leo. Last year, as we crossed Piazza della Signoria in Florence one evening, there was an opera singer holding a concert in a loggia. Could we linger to hear her sing, I asked him? No. He was ready to call it a day, and the unearthly beauty of the aria in such a gorgeous setting was lost on him. The next morning, I reminded myself that Leo is still a kid. This was clear when we embarked on a hike with my close friend, Giovanni. During the long car ride to his house, Leo complained, and by the time I greeted Giovanni and his wife, Veronica, in Italian, he seemed somewhat sullen, tuning us out. I began to worry; would this be one more frustrating afternoon? But then it emerged that Giovanni was bringing a dog named Dante along with us. Leo reached for Dante’s leash immediately and took charge of walking him during our long hike in the mountains outside of the Tuscan city of Pistoia. As we hiked, I could hear Leo beckoning to the dog, “Here, Dante, here boy. Who’s a good boy?” In the end, he was a 13-year-old American boy far from home — and his own dog — who needed a simple pleasure that had nothing to do with Renaissance art. He just wanted a dog to play with — and woof-woof was a language he understood. Moments of pure delight The trips, of course, have offered far more than compromises. On our way to a rented house in Puglia, in Southern Italy, during our 2018 trip, we stopped for gas around lunchtime. The service station, which was in a small town on the Adriatic Coast, also housed a restaurant. Good food is everywhere in Italy — even at highway rest stops — so after filling the gas tank, we sat down to eat at a table outside and I ordered spaghetti alle vongole — pasta with clams, an Italian seaside specialty. From our table, I could see the gas pumps, and also a selection of cheap beach toys for sale in the service station market. I’d never eaten at a gas station. But it didn’t take long before I declared it the best spaghetti dish I’ve ever had. Leo laughed out loud. “You had good spaghetti at a gas station, Mommy. A gas station!” During a later trip, we rented an apartment in Rome that had a typical Italian elevator, where you could clearly observe the pulleys hoisting the cabin up and down. Located beside the central staircase, the elevator had double swinging doors and a metal grate, all of which had to be carefully closed if we wanted the elevator to move. Leo took charge of “operating” the elevator, eagerly pressing the button to call for it, and then closing the doors once we were aboard. Children naturally unlock experiences, especially in Italy. Once in Florence, we stayed at a friend’s apartment that overlooks a private park belonging to the exclusive Four Seasons Hotel. My friend said we could enter the park, which is studded with period sculptures, just by visiting the café inside. Yet since the hotel was quite swanky, I hesitated when Leo and I arrived at the entrance, giving no thought to his t-shirt, which was emblazoned with the city’s soccer club logo and the team’s signature purple color. But when I asked the doorman, the born-and-bred Florentine looked at Leo’s Fiorentina shirt, and exclaimed, “In that shirt, he can go wherever he wants!” I suspect more compromises are ahead. But what about the payoff? Will he eventually become fluent in Italian? Will he live there as I did, an expat in thrall to the language of Dante (the poet, not the dog)? Only time will tell. For now, he knows the Italian word for cuckold and has a taste for Ferrari merchandise. I can imagine him one day exchanging the quadricycle from the Villa Borghese for a fast Italian car — maybe one that he could use to drive us around our favorite country. None of us would be compromising.
