articles.title: Former NFL team doctor addresses Jalen Hurts' blood clot as QB's season hinges on one key word
articles.summary: Dr. David Chao explains why one word in the Eagles' statement about Jalen Hurts' blood clot could signal a long-term or season-ending absence.
articles.body: David Chao served as the Chargers team doctor for 17 years while they were still in San Diego, so when he studied the statement the Philadelphia Eagles released about Jalen Hurts and his blood clot, the doctor focused on one key word that will determine whether the quarterback misses a little time or a long time. The word that glowed in neon for Dr. Chao was "movement." The Eagles' statement announcing Hurts is out for Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers said that a follow-up ultrasound on Wednesday revealed "movement in the small blood clot" the team had discovered four days earlier. CAROLINA PANTHERS LINEMAN TAYLOR MOTON OVERCAME BLOODY, LIFE-THREATENING EPISODE AND NOW HE'S BACK AT PRACTICE That blood clot discovered on Saturday was described by the team as "superficial." "What do they mean by movement?" Dr. Chao told OutKick. "Do they mean movement as in it's propagating and it's now a bigger superficial blood clot? Or is it movement meaning it's deeper and it's a deep vein clot? "If he has a deep vein clot, he's out for multiple weeks, at least." Dr. Chao explained superficial clots can indeed move. They can move and remain superficial. "But if movement means it has become deep vein, then he's out long term, and they haven't revealed the whole breadth or depth of the news yet," he added. By "deep vein," Dr. Chao means a deep vein thrombosis. If Hurts has a deep vein thrombosis in his leg, missing one game on Sunday would be only the start of a long and possibly season-ending absence. "If it's a deep vein thrombosis it starts to be measured in months not weeks," Dr. Chao said. That's not all. A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) clot can break loose. It can travel through the bloodstream to the lungs and block blood flow. That's known as a pulmonary embolism. "Then he would be out for the season," Dr. Chao said. A pulmonary embolism requires strong anticoagulation medicine. And no doctor would clear Hurts to play while taking such medication. Why can't a player play if he is on strong anticoagulants? The risk of bleeding. No, a player is not going to have a medical emergency from a scratch that won't stop bleeding. But there is other bleeding that must be considered. PACKERS RECEIVER JAYDEN REED GETS BAD NEWS ABOUT NECK INJURY AFTER LEAVING WEEK 2 GAME ON SPINE BOARD "Internal organ bleeding would be worrisome, but the big fear is, what if you have a brain bleed?" said Dr. Chao, who is the founder of the sports injury insights site SICScore.com. Dr. Chao said going on anticoagulants does not automatically keep Hurts from being cleared to play. The issue is the strength of the anticoagulant he might require. The Eagles, it should be noted, said they first discovered Hurts' blood clot by doing an ultrasound after they flew to London on Saturday. The clot at that time was "superficial" and it was decided Hurts could play. Then the team flew back to Philadelphia after the game and on Wednesday evening a new ultrasound discovered the "movement" that caused the team to rule Hurts out against the Panthers. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! So did the flight back from London make the quarterback's condition worse? "I hear you," Dr. Chao said. "But it depends what they did for the flight. If they said, 'Oh, nothing to see here, don't worry about it,' that would raise an eyebrow. "You have to understand, people with superficial DVTs get sent home and do sleep at night and that's sometimes eight hours. He's not in a seat that can't move. If they urged him to move, they had some sort of pulsatile device on his leg, they had compression stockings, blood thinned it a little bit, then the flight is very defensible. "If they said nothing to see here, it causes at least an eyebrow raise." FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

articles.title: ‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
articles.summary: Forged signatures and thumbprints – even of dead and fictitious people – allegedly used to obtain land for bauxite mine.
articles.body:
Koraput, India – Raghunath Khara was shocked to look at his thumb impression on a piece of paper that declared he had consented to a government proposal to mine his village’s pristine forest land for bauxite.

He says he never gave that thumb impression.

“I always sign in English. It was someone else’s thumb,” alleged Khara, a shopkeeper in Balda village in the tribal-dominated Koraput district of Odisha state in eastern India.

Khara is among hundreds of people from Indigenous tribes in Balda and neighbouring Bannur village who have lost their lands to the new bauxite mine. It is being developed by Kalinga Alumina Limited, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises Limited, a conglomerate owned by Gautam Adani, India’s second richest businessman and close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The $24m project will consume a large chunk of the tabletop Balda Hill – home to forests, grasslands and caves that are considered sacred by at least 10 tribal villages surrounding it.

To push the project, the purported signatures and thumb impressions of nearly 600 tribals were allegedly collected during village council meetings in Balda and Bannur held on October 9 last year. Bannur is 5km from Balda.

Khara says he never attended the meeting at Balda and was instead protesting against the proposed mine with his wife, sister and other villagers about 100 metres from the village council office.

“It [thumb impression] was fake. We didn’t attend the village meeting at all. We were all busy protesting outside,” he told Al Jazeera.

India’s constitution recognises the rights of Indigenous communities over their traditional lands. Forest laws and laws granting autonomy to tribal areas dictate that village council resolutions are mandatory for any diversion of such lands for other purposes.

A resolution passed in a village council meeting is valid only if 50 percent of all the adults in the village consent to it in writing. Government documents claim all the 580 adults – 360 in Balda and 227 in Bannur – agreed to give up their land for the Adani mine. But the elected village heads in both villages denied any signatures were collected and called the two meetings “invalid”.

Even photographs taken by villagers at both council meetings show a combined attendance of about 100 people – nearly 40 in Balda and 68 in Bannur – far below the minimum 50 percent quorum required to pass a valid resolution.

Moreover, the villagers allege that most signatures on the resolution documents are fake, forged or impersonated.

They also claim the documents contain signatures of fictitious persons and even the names of people who died years ago. Some even said their signatures from a previous, unrelated village council meeting were fraudulently pasted onto the bauxite mine document.

Al Jazeera emailed the Adani group and its communications chief on August 18 seeking responses to the accusations of forgery and fraud. Then we followed up with a second request for comments on September 25, but did not receive any response. Al Jazeera also sought responses from Manoj Satyawan Mahajan, the district magistrate — the most senior bureaucrat in Koraput – to the concerns raised by villagers but did not receive a response. Rohit Varma, the superintendent of police for Koraput district, also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s queries.

Many of those who attended the meetings said they were opposed to the mining project.

“We were told that if mining was allowed, the village would get roads, jobs, drainage and water connections and a school built,” said Madhav Kuntili, a farmer in Bannur.

Koraput is one of India’s least developed districts and similar promises often have a significant sway. Kuntili said a document was passed around, seeking signatures.

“I said if the forest was being diverted, then I would not sign it. They took the paper away from me,” he told Al Jazeera.

Across Balda and Bannur, Al Jazeera met many villagers who said they were shocked to find their signatures or thumb impressions on the resolution.

Rama Hantal sat motionless by the doorway of his rusted tin-and-wood hut. The 60-year-old has been paralysed for several years and is unable to talk.

“There is no chance he could have attended the meeting or even signed,” said Chandrama Hantal, his daughter-in-law.

While Hantal had apparently signed the consent form in Odia, Odisha’s official language, Chandrama saw a thumb impression against her name. She also denied attending the meeting.

Among the signatories are three Gurubari Kharas – their purported thumb impressions in support of the mining project.

In Balda, villagers could only track two “Gurubaris” – one living 3km away who denied attending the meeting – and another from the village itself, who had died well before the village council meeting was held.

“My mother died in February 2025. How can they forge her presence and signature eight months later?” asked her son, Sahdev. She was nearly 75 when she died of natural causes.

Two other persons from the first Gurubari’s family are also listed as signatories – her bedridden husband, who has been paralysed since falling from a tree three months before the council meeting and her nephew. Both deny attending the October 9 meeting.

Al Jazeera interviewed more than 20 people and accessed records from both Balda and Bannur villages, but could not trace at least 67 persons named as signatories in the resolution.

In Bannur, at least three deceased persons were represented through thumbprints. The families of all three – who are also listed in the documents as consenters – confirmed the deaths of their kin.

“My mother died four years ago,” said Nakul Alang, the 35-year-old son of Sanai Alang who is listed at serial number 108 in the Bannur resolution.

Nakul’s signature appears in Odia, but he says he was working at a construction site in Visakhapatnam, a coastal city in Odisha’s neighbouring Andhra Pradesh state 170km (105 miles) from Koraput.

“I don’t know who put our names and signatures,” he told Al Jazeera.

On page 10 of the 16-page Bannur resolution document, 13 names are written by the same hand, followed by a neat array of thumb impressions next to them.

When Sunadhar Muduli, a 50-year-old farmer, saw the sheet, he immediately recognised that it was his own handwriting.

“But none of us ever attended the Gram Sabha meeting,” he said.

Muduli said Ramnath Pungi, who works for the local revenue office on contract, visited the village in December and handed him a registry. He was asked to fill the names of those residents who wanted to get their traditional lands recognised by the government.

Many tribal communities, who have been historically kept out of land documentation, have been cultivating on “government-owned” lands for generations. There have been frequent promises to transfer such lands to their names, and it is not uncommon practice in the region to send contracted officials to collect information about farmers.

“He said he needed everyone’s signatures. I told him I would gather the residents, but he said that was not necessary. That I could sign on their behalf,” said Muduli, who then called some residents to get their permission.

“I wrote down the names on one side of the page and then he and I placed our thumbs alternatively against the name. It was his idea and I just followed the instructions,” he said.

It was only in June when Al Jazeera visited Bannur that Muduli saw the inclusion of the same sheet as part of the mining resolution draft.

Pungi also confirmed to Al Jazeera that the signatures were taken on another pretext.

“I was paid 3,000 rupees to collect documents and sign land settlement documents from each village. That’s what I did. I only submitted the signed sheet to the [revenue] office,” he said.

“I did not know they would use it for this [Adani project]. I am also against mining in our region.”

Official guidelines state that the announcement of a Gram Sabha meeting should be made two weeks before the scheduled date in order to ensure a quorum.

However, several residents told Al Jazeera that the notices announcing the meeting were pasted outside the village council offices on October 8, only a day before the meeting. The notices, accessed by Al Jazeera, were dated September 22 and September 23, 2025.

Meanwhile, the government pushed the Adani mining project in Odisha – hastily, according to the residents and activists.

In February 2023, the Odisha government declared Adani Enterprises as the preferred bidder for the mine at Koraput, triggering immediate protests by the tribal people in Balda and Bannur. They marched to the local government office to protest against the mining of 157 hectares of forest land by destroying the trees around them and displacing residents.

Two years later, on March 6, 2025, the state government held a public hearing – a mandatory process to obtain approvals where villagers are given details of the project and their objections formally recorded. An overwhelming number of villagers expressed their opposition to the mining project.

Despite the objections, an environmental clearance – a key approval given by the government after assessing possible ecological damage of a project – was granted a few months later.

Under Indian laws, forest-dwelling communities who have been historically left out of land -ownership can seek individual or community rights over traditional forest lands. Balda and neighbouring communities applied for rights over 2,500 hectares of forest land in 2025. A majority of those claims overlapped with the mining lease area.

Usually, the settlement of claims involves the collation of claims and documents, approval from local bodies, verification by officials and ample time for appeals if the claims are modified or rejected. The process is usually notoriously slow.

In January, authorities “settled” these community rights claims without informing the village councils in the area. Less than one-fifth of the claimed area was recognised while the entirety of the mining area was excluded from the claims. Villagers are usually given time to appeal.

However, in this case, two appeals committees affirmed the decision in just three days, without even allowing the villagers time to submit their appeals, allege the villagers.

Ajaya Muduli is part of a three-member team authorised by the affected villages to approach any court in India, sign documents, take necessary legal steps and liaise with government committees in their fight to prevent the takeover of their lands.

Muduli told Al Jazeera that the land acquisition process was “abnormally rushed”.

“We have safeguarded this sacred land for centuries and yet were not even consulted,” Muduli told Al Jazeera. “This is a clear tactic forcing the mines on us without our consent while snatching our rights.”

Immediately after the October 9 Gram Sabha meetings, the villagers wrote to the local authorities asking for the deliberations to be held again. They flagged the hurried nature of the meetings and pointed to the fact that the village heads had declared them “invalid”.

Yet, on October 15, the allegedly forged resolutions were added to the official file. It was only on February 11 this year that those documents were made public on the environment ministry’s website.

So far, more than 50 people from several villages in Koraput have issued sworn affidavits declaring that they did not attend the village council meetings and that their signatures or thumb impressions were forged. They have also filed petitions in court and with district authorities, as well as complaints with the police, alleging forgery and demanding an investigation into the land given for the Adani mine.

In March, the 10 affected villages around Balda Hill held meetings where they rejected the previous resolutions passed by their village councils and reiterated their opposition to the proposed bauxite mine.

In May, Muduli approached the court on behalf of the villagers. But it was too late.

On May 7, all required approvals were granted to Kalinga Alumina Limited and the forest land was handed over for the $24m bauxite mining project, with an associated alumina refinery on a lease of 50 years. No compensation has been promised to the villagers.

“What they have done is illegal, but we will not back off,” Balda resident Rajendra Khara told Al Jazeera.

While the approvals have been granted, actual work has not started on the ground. Villagers have vowed to stop construction. “Whatever happens, we are never going to give it to Adani. This is our ancestral land,” Rajendra said.

Arpitha Kodiveri, assistant professor of political science at Vassar College in the United States who has worked on environmental law and justice related to mining in India, told Al Jazeera that bypassing the consent of landowners sets a trend for illegal practice.

“What you are starting to see across multiple jurisdictions is an administrative approach to bypassing the consent provision. What I fear is that it has become an illegal administrative practice of implementing the consent provision without adhering to procedure and law, and that is something we should be worried about,” she said.

Kodiveri said alleged irregularities in the consent process could also provide grounds for the affected parties to challenge the government clearance granted to such mining projects. She also argued that the rules should make consequences for irregular consent practices clearer and must seek accountability when mandatory provisions are bypassed.

“Guidelines must be established so this process is implemented in spirit and not just in letter, and to signal to administrative actors that there are consequences for practising fraudulent signatures or taking signatures of the deceased. This has happened so many times in Odisha and elsewhere that it is a deeply troubling trend.”

Land Conflict Watch, a New Delhi-based research organisation, has tracked at least 28 instances of consent-related “conflicts” from projects such as mining, plantation, energy and other infrastructure across India since 2003. The organisation also found allegations of forgery, evasion of mandatory public consultations and forceful mining of ancestral land while studying such conflicts.

Even the studies conducted by the government show a similar trend.

A 2024 report by India’s Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), an independent constitutional authority, on land management in tribal-dominated areas revealed 136 consent violations in mining and other projects. In 73 of these violations, no Gram Sabha meetings were held, while in another 29, land acquisition was done while disregarding the views of the village council.

Over the past few years, however, allegations of outright forgeries of Gram Sabha resolutions have emerged.

In 2023 in Sijimali, about 180km from Balda, villagers discovered similar forged consents and meetings for a bauxite mine by Vedanta Resources, India’s largest mining company backed by a London-based conglomerate. At least eight villages denied consent to hand over 708 hectares of forest land, despite official documents claiming otherwise.

Sijimali has seen near-continuous protests since, escalating to violence in April when clashes between the police and protesters injured 70.

“If the Gram Sabha has not given consent, then the forest clearance given is illegal. It has to be quashed. They are making a mockery of the law,” Shomona Khanna, a Supreme Court lawyer specialising in environmental and tribal law, told Al Jazeera.

“These are criminal offences … Any person who dispossesses a forest dweller of their forest right or interferes in the enjoyment of the forest right is committing a crime, which is called an atrocity under Indian law,” she said.

Back in Balda, the villagers fear that if mining starts, the rainwater-fed streams that sustain paddy cultivation will dry up. Forests that provided gourds, fruits, flowers, bark, firewood and medicinal plants will be affected.

Like many Indigenous tribal communities, their animist faith is linked to the surrounding forests – home to small shrines, idols and caves considered to be sacred.

“The forest is everything for us,” said Raghunath Hanthal, a 70-year-old priest in Balda. “Our maa [goddess] is here.”

On the official document, the priest’s name is listed as serial number 171, with his purported signature in Odia.

“I did not even go to the meeting. We were here, protesting that day,” he said. “Taking away our forests will not just destroy our livelihood, but it will incur the wrath of our goddess.”

articles.title: Indian police again detain ‘cockroach’ movement founder ahead of protest
articles.summary: Police detained India’s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief.
articles.body: Police detained India’s “cockroach” movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief. The youth-led “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP), opposition groups, and student organizations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban. The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag. The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away. “We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke. “I have not broken any law right now…how can you detain me,” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away. There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention. Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: A shopper paid just £1 at a UK car boot sale for a 1953 first-edition Casino Royale in its original dust jacket; after experts recognised the rare James Bond book, it sold at auction for £10,000
articles.summary: A book bought for just £1 at a UK car boot sale turned out to be a rare first edition of Casino Royale, the 1953 novel that introduced readers to James
articles.body: A book bought for just £1 at a UK car boot sale turned out to be a rare first edition of Casino Royale, the 1953 novel that introduced readers to James Bond. The copy, which retained its original dust jacket, eventually sold for £10,000 at auction, turning an ordinary second-hand purchase into a remarkable discovery. According to the Antiques Trade Gazette, the buyer had picked up the book while visiting family in Yorkshire around 10 years before the auction. The story highlights how overlooked books can command substantial sums when their edition, condition and publishing history make them desirable to collectors.A forgotten purchase revealed a rare findThe buyer, a woman from Torquay, purchased the book while visiting family in Yorkshire. She was not a book collector and did not initially recognise the significance of the title. What caught her attention was the pink hearts on the cover.The book subsequently remained inside a box for years. When she eventually began clearing out her belongings, she came across the old purchase and searched for its title online. Realising it could be valuable, she contacted Chris Surfleet of auction house Adam Partridge, who identified it as a clean first edition with its original dust jacket. The auction house announced the discovery on June 11, 2024, estimating that the book could fetch between £10,000 and £15,000. It was scheduled to go under the hammer at the Devon saleroom on June 24.Why the original dust jacket matteredThe book's value lay in more than its age. Casino Royale was published by Jonathan Cape in 1953 and introduced Ian Fleming's fictional British secret agent, James Bond, also known as 007. The novel follows Bond on a mission involving a high-stakes baccarat game against Le Chiffre, an agent working for the Soviet intelligence service.The auctioned copy was a first edition, first impression, retaining its original dust jacket. According to the Antiques Trade Gazette, the absence of a Times review on the front flap helped identify the dust jacket as a first-state version used on early copies. Although the jacket had a few minor tears, its survival added to the book's appeal. It also retained the original price of 10 shillings and sixpence on both the front and rear flaps. According to Adam Partridge, the 1953 edition was one of only 4,750 copies printed.From a £1 bargain to a £10,000 auction saleThe book went under the hammer at Adam Partridge's Devon saleroom on June 24, 2024. It sold for £10,000, the lower end of its estimated range of £10,000 to £15,000. The amount was the hammer price, before the buyer's premium. The successful bidder was a UK buyer who specialised in collecting rare Ian Fleming editions and participated by telephone, Antiques Trade Gazette reported.The sale also illustrated how condition can influence the value of a collectible. Although the original dust jacket survived, its minor tears may have prevented the book from fetching a higher price, auctioneer Chris Surfleet told the Antiques Trade Gazette. Comparable first editions had previously sold for £10,000 and £17,000 at Forum Auctions, while a particularly fine copy fetched £22,500 in 2017.For the woman who bought it without knowing its significance, the book had remained an ordinary second-hand purchase for years. Its eventual sale demonstrated how a modest find can become a sought-after collectible when rarity, condition and publishing history come together.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: You're probably cooking rice wrong, and chefs reveal the simple mistake to avoid
articles.summary: Chefs reveal why rinsing basmati and jasmine rice before cooking is the key to fluffy, distinct grains that never clump together in the pot.
articles.body: Rice may be a kitchen staple, but cooking it well at home can be trickier than it seems. Experts say the trick to tender rice with distinct grains that stay separate instead of clumping together may begin before you even turn on the stove, with a step many home cooks skip. "I generally rinse before cooking when I want a light, fluffy result," Dennis Littley, a New Jersey-based classically trained chef and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital. FOUR FOODS YOU SHOULD NEVER STORE IN THE FREEZER — AND WHERE TO KEEP THEM INSTEAD He recommends rinsing long-grain white rice, basmati and jasmine rice until the water goes from very cloudy to mostly clear. It doesn't need to be perfectly transparent, he said. The rinse removes some of the loose surface starch that can make rice gummy or clumpy, Littley said. Then, drain it well so the water-to-rice ratio is not thrown off. But chefs also note that not every type of rice should be treated the same. CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS IF YOU CAN DRIVE TO MCDONALD'S, YOU CAN COOK HEALTHY MEALS AT HOME "The important thing is to adjust your technique for the type of rice you're using rather than applying one method to every variety," Littley said. Christine Pittman, the Florida-based founder and CEO of COOKtheStory, TheCookful and COOKforTWO, said she reserves the rinse for short-grain rice and for when she is cooking rice in a pressure cooker. Littley and Pittman both suggest skipping the rinse for risotto, noting that the starch helps make the dish creamy. THE BEST CHEESE FOR A BURGER, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT — AND WHY SOME POPULAR PICKS FALL FLAT A recent side-by-side test by Food & Wine found that rinsed and soaked basmati and jasmine rice were lighter and fluffier than unwashed rice, which clumped together. The test combined rinsing and soaking, not rinsing alone. "I especially like soaking basmati rice for about 20 to 30 minutes before cooking," Littley said. "It helps the grains hydrate evenly and can give you longer, more distinct grains with a nice fluffy texture." There are other ways home cooks can improve their rice, too. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Pittman recommends a little less than 2 cups of water for every 1 cup of long-grain white rice but says the amount varies by variety. For Japanese-style short-grain white rice, a rough stovetop starting point is 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 cups of water per cup of rice. Littley likewise advises following the package or recipe directions for the specific rice. While brown rice can also be rinsed, its bran layer means it needs more water — about 2 cups per 1 cup of rice — and more time to cook. Briefly toasting rice in a little oil or butter after rinsing and draining, but before adding liquid, can add a nutty flavor and help keep the grains defined, Littley said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Once the rice and cooking liquid are in the pot and the liquid comes to a boil, lower the heat to a gentle simmer and cover the pot, Littley said, and avoid lifting the lid or stirring while it cooks, Littley said. When the rice is done, take it off the heat and let it rest, covered, for five to 10 minutes before fluffing with a fork. Letting it rest allows moisture to redistribute for a more even texture. "Overcooked rice is bad, but my hot take is that undercooked rice is worse." She recommends fluffing it with a dinner fork, using a "gentle folding motion" to lift the rice from the bottom of the pot rather than stirring it vigorously. articles.summary: A Norwegian teenager who planned to commit murder in Britain after ​being recruited by a Swedish organised ‌crime group linked to the Iranian government was on Friday sentenced to 20 years’ detention.
articles.body: A Norwegian teenager who planned to commit murder in Britain after ​being recruited by a Swedish organised ‌crime group linked to the Iranian government was on Friday sentenced to 20 years’ detention. Johannes Natland, ​now 19, was arrested in a ​hotel room in Huddersfield, northern England, ⁠in March 2025 with two firearms and ​ammunition in his possession. Natland was recruited by ​the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group used by the Iranian state and sanctioned by ​both Britain and the United States, ​prosecutors said. He admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver ‌and ⁠ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder and claimed he did not intend to carry out the plan. But he was convicted in ​July after a ​retrial ⁠and was sentenced at London’s Woolwich Crown Court to detention for ​20 years. Natland was the latest ​young ⁠adult to stand trial in Britain and elsewhere over serious criminal acts allegedly carried ⁠out ​after being recruited online ​for money, often as an unwitting proxy for a foreign state.

articles.title: Why is China buying up gold?
articles.summary: Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say.
articles.body:
China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy.

The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.

Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government.

But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know.

China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024.

Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold.

Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month.

The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not.

A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera.

The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible.

The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said.

“I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks.

America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold.

Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said.

The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.

Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.”

But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed.

“The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially.

Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves.

China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said.

“The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.”

Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council.

Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024.

Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.

articles.title: Norwegian teen sentenced to 20 years for U.K. murder plot tied to Iran-linked gang
articles.summary: A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.
articles.body: A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison. Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot an unknown target for 25,000 euros (21,500 pounds) last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield in northern England with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K. The target is not known. Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to counterterrorism officers from London’s Metropolitan Police. Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he did not want to go through with the plan. “You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself,” Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said at his sentencing hearing at Woolwich Crown Court in southeast London. “Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to.” Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as “Generalen.” A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to “contribute to murder” and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy. The U.K. government last year announced sanctions against Foxtrot Network and its leader “due to their involvement in violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime.” The sanctions include an asset freeze that bars U.K. businesses from handling funds or other economic assets controlled by the organization.

articles.title: ‘Trying to dominate’: In Cyprus, some fear Israel’s growing influence
articles.summary: Israel now reaches into Cyprus’s water, gas, health and defence and many Cypriots fear their island is losing control.
articles.body:
Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory.

He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments.

Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily.

Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems.

Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield.

Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus.

Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without.

Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis.

Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea.

With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department.

Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year.

Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital.

For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line.

“It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said.

Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said.

In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements.

Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements.

“Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said.

Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said.

At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast.

Investors in Israel held 5.1 billion euros ($5.7bn) of investment in Cyprus at the end of 2024, more than six times what they held in 2017, according to the Central Bank of Cyprus.

The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace.

The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is also weighing a bid for the Cyprus Stock Exchange, which the government is privatising, Cyprus Mail and the Israeli business daily Globes reported this month.

The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail.

Hadassah Medical Centre Limassol, the Israeli hospital group’s first centre in Europe, began seeing patients in July and was formally opened on Thursday.

Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America.

Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters.

Israel has also been flexing its military muscle.

Israeli special forces have trained in Cyprus’s Troodos mountains, whose terrain resembles southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies.

In 2022, the two armies held their largest joint exercise yet, simulating a war with Hezbollah, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Cyprus is replacing its Russian-made air defences with the Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, with deliveries beginning in late 2024.

Israel presents itself as a guardian against Turkiye.

Following a coup in Cyprus backed by Greece’s military government in July 1974, Turkiye invaded the island and has occupied its northern part ever since. Only Turkiye and its Turkish Cypriot leadership recognise Northern Cyprus.

In late December 2025, Israeli and Cypriot military officials signed a 2026 cooperation plan covering joint exercises, training, and “strategic military dialogue”, the Israeli military said.

On Tuesday, a pro-Israel advocacy group, the Israel Allies Foundation (IAF), launched a caucus of six Cypriot lawmakers from three parties in Nicosia. Its president, Josh Reinstein, told reporters after the group’s meeting with the Cypriot president at the presidential palace on Wednesday that Turkiye is a “common adversary”, according to the Cyprus Mail.

The opposition party AKEL called it “extremely provocative”, asking what credibility Cyprus has in demanding pressure on Turkiye while backing “another occupying and settler state”, the Cyprus Mail reported.

Last month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “illegally occupies northern Cyprus, an EU member”.

Netanyahu “knows what he’s doing”, said Ioanna Lamprou, a writer in Limassol.

Cypriots who feel the world has forgotten the occupation , she said, will “become more sympathetic to Israel and to Netanyahu’s government because of this”, but they “don’t understand that what’s happening in the West Bank is illegal occupation as well”.

Laou understands the government’s reasoning; from its perspective, she said, “Cyprus can’t protect itself from anything.”

Ceylan Hassan, a Turkish Cypriot researcher and environmental social scientist, said the British had won over Cypriots the same way, by promising to keep them safe from a bigger threat.

Israel is doing “the whole colonial thing of let’s create a problem and then be the solution to it and never let it go”.

In 1902, Theodore Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, presented a pamphlet to a British Parliamentary Committee with the idea of establishing a Jewish homeland in Cyprus. He offered a pamphlet with the title: The problem of Jewish immigration to England and the United States solved by furthering the Jewish Colonisation of Cyprus.

Britain’s colonial secretary refused, saying Greeks and Muslims lived there, according to Herzl’s diary.

Herzl mused, “The Greeks will gladly sell their lands at a good price and migrate to Athens or Crete.”

Achniotis has thought about that history more since the genocidal war on Gaza began.

Watching what is happening to Palestinians, he said, “I think it can happen to anyone.”

As the onslaught happened so easily, with the acceptance of the US and European governments, “you feel a kind of insecurity,” he said. “Why are they going to respect you?”

articles.title: Hawick guest house partially washed away by flood up for sale
articles.summary: Dramatic footage captured part of the building in Hawick collapsing into the water during Storm Ciara.
articles.body:
A Hawick guest house and cafe that was partially washed away in floods has gone on the market.

Video footage captured the moment river-facing walls of the Bridge Guest House building dramatically collapsed into the Teviot at the height of Storm Ciara in February 2020.

At the time, owner Gino Antonacci told the BBC that he had managed to get all guests out as river levels continued to rise and cracks began to appear in the walls.

The remains of the seven-bedroom property have a guide price of £40,000.

Although Hawick had been hit by several large floods in the decade before Storm Ciara, the Bridge Guest House had not been affected.

However, as water levels rose on 8 February 2020, cracks began to appear - with large sections falling into the river the following morning.

Antonacci added: "We had some signs of the wall going under the water.

"There were cracks coming in the wall, so we evacuated the premises.

"At night the river was very strong and high - and in the morning it just collapsed."

Since the collapse of the Bridge Guest House, a £106m flood defence scheme has been completed in Hawick, protecting about 970 buildings.

Work began on the project - one of the largest in Scotland - a few months after Storm Ciara.

It has been designed to protect about 1,000 homes from a one-in-75-year event and consists of about two miles (3km) of flood defences.

Although some of the old building has gone, the remainder - now surrounded by high walls - still has seven en-suite bedrooms over two floors, although little is left of the cafe.

Selling agents Jim Hay stated: "The property is being sold as seen, and any new building must be within the original footprint of the existing building."

articles.title: Five siblings fought over their late mother’s trust and property income; California court rules rental proceeds cannot reduce inheritance shares
articles.summary: A California inheritance dispute involving five siblings, decades of family loans and rental income, and several property transactions centred mainly on
articles.body: A California inheritance dispute involving five siblings, decades of family loans and rental income, and several property transactions centred mainly on how much a trustee could deduct from a beneficiary’s share of an inheritance. In Sandford v. Sandford, decided on September 2, 2026, the California Court of Appeal ruled that a trust’s equalisation clause allowed deductions for unpaid loans and unequal gifts, but not for rental or property-sale proceeds. The decision reversed a substantial part of an Orange County trial court’s ruling, which had treated various financial benefits as early distributions and ordered them deducted from two brothers’ shares. The appellate court upheld the orders on unpaid loans and left other parts of the judgment intact.Sandford v. Sandford: five siblings, quitclaim deeds and family financesAccording to the published appellate opinion, Jean and Dean Sandford had five children: Michael, Mark, Linda, Debra and Pamela. Dean died without a will in 1988. Jean disclaimed part of her interest in Dean’s half of the community property, and that portion was distributed among their five children, giving them interests in family properties. In 1993, the siblings signed quitclaim deeds transferring their interests in the Center Street property to Jean. Similar deeds were executed for the Quincy property in 1995. The documents described the transfers as inter-family transactions for no consideration. The family later disputed whether the deeds transferred full beneficial ownership or were intended to facilitate refinancing. Jean established a trust in 1998, naming Debra, Pamela and Linda as successor trustees. In a 2000 restatement, she added Michael and Mark to that role. The operative trust provided for equal distributions but included an equalisation clause covering unpaid loans and unequal gifts. Under its terms, unpaid loans to a child or that child’s family were to be included in the child’s share, while unequal gifts were to be treated as advances against an equal inheritance.The siblings gradually assumed responsibilities for Jean’s finances and properties. Linda managed her personal accounts and bills, while Mark handled rental accounts. Michael, a lawyer, represented the family in connection with the Anaheim School District’s efforts to acquire the Wilken Way fourplex through eminent domain. The property was sold in 2008, generating approximately $829,000 in net proceeds. The opinion also describes loans Jean made to her sons, including a $60,000 loan to Michael in the early 1990s for a helicopter-related investment. Jean died in October 2014. Debra and Linda filed a court petition in May 2018 seeking an accounting, removal of Michael and Mark as trustees, and other relief. Michael and Mark filed their own petition in July 2019. In March 2020, the court suspended the co-trustees’ powers and appointed an independent temporary trustee.Orange County trial court: a 20-year review of family transactionsThe trial lasted 22 nonconsecutive days and resulted in a 64-page statement of decision. The trial court generally found Linda and Debra credible and Michael and Mark not credible. It removed Michael and Mark as trustees and ordered an accounting of trust assets in their possession from 2009 through 2020. The court also interpreted the equalisation clause broadly, treating various rental and sale proceeds as early distributions that should reduce the brothers’ inheritance shares. It ordered deductions for unpaid loans, including the $60,000 helicopter-related loan, as well as property income.For Center Street, the court treated $537,930 in rent collected by Mark from 2002 through 2020 as an early distribution. It also attributed $601,560 in rental proceeds from the Orange Park property to Mark. For the Quincy property, it ordered $145,620 each in deductions for Michael and Mark, representing half of the rental proceeds over the period considered. The court rejected Debra and Linda’s financial elder abuse and breach of fiduciary duty claims as time-barred. It nevertheless ordered the trustee to make adjustments under the equalisation clause and awarded attorney fees to Debra and Linda from trust assets. Pamela had settled her claims before trial and was not a party to the appeal.California appeals court: the trust clause covered loans and gifts, not property proceedsThe California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three, held that the trial court had interpreted the equalisation provision too broadly. Its September 2, 2026, opinion said the clause’s ordinary meaning covered unpaid loans and gifts, not every financial benefit a beneficiary might have received. The appellate court rejected the use of the clause to deduct rental and sale proceeds. It explained that any claims arising from alleged misconduct in those property transactions were subject to the statute of limitations, as the trial court had already found. The court explained that the trial court could not circumvent the applicable limitations periods by adopting an interpretation of the trust that conflicted with its plain language.The court reached a different conclusion on unpaid loans. Citing Cook v. Cook (2009), it upheld the orders concerning unpaid loans, which included a $60,000 helicopter-related loan in the trial court’s orders. It held that the trust required unpaid loans to be accounted for when distributing the inheritance, even if a lawsuit to collect a debt might be time-barred. The appellate court also upheld the denial of Mark’s claim to quiet title to the Center Street property. Mark argued that his quitclaim deed transferred only legal title, but the trial court found that he had failed to prove his claim by clear and convincing evidence and did not believe his testimony. On appeal, the court held that the evidence did not compel a finding in Mark’s favour as a matter of law, given the trial court’s adverse credibility finding and his failure of proof. The court affirmed the judgment in other respects and reversed the orders that treated rental and sale proceeds as early distributions. It also reversed the attorney-fee awards, leaving the fee question open for further proceedings. Michael and Mark were awarded their costs on appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: A Florida man allegedly slashed a 70-year-old Publix shopper with a box cutter just over three months after a mental health court ended his probation early in a case involving an unprovoked attack on a teenager. According to the Punta Gorda Police Department, Ramsey Thomas Lyons, 47, faces a felony charge of aggravated battery on a person 65 years or older following an attack at the Publix Super Market on Tamiami Trail in Punta Gorda on Oct. 10. A sworn probable cause arrest affidavit indicated that Lyons approached a man from behind, shortly before 4 p.m. while David Terry shopped inside the store. After feeling someone violently strike him, the victim turned to face Lyons, who allegedly stared at him while holding a box cutter blade. The victim ran to the front of the store after touching his head and noticing his hands were bloody, the affidavit stated. FLORIDA MEN WIELDING HATCHET AND MACHETE CLASH IN PUBLIX PARKING LOT, POLICE SAY Punta Gorda police officers arrived and apprehended Lyons at the front of the store, where he stood with his hands on his head. They also recovered a box cutter from the aisle where the incident occurred. OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO First responders took the victim to Fawcett Memorial Hospital with a severe cut measuring four to six inches from his left cheek down to his neck, alongside a minor laceration to his upper chest, police said. Lyons, who waived his Miranda rights, told authorities that he had a deep "dislike for the 1960s era," and admitted he planned to kill someone in the store that day. He targeted the victim solely because the shopper "looked like he was from the 1960s" and felt like "acing him out," police said. WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE "I just pulled it out of my pocket and stuck it in his neck," Lyons said, according to the affidavit. Lyons, who told police he had mental health issues, allegedly admitted he spent two days planning the attack and that he purposely dropped the weapon down the aisle so that responding officers would not use a Taser or shoot him. MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE The attack renewed criticism from the mother of a teenager Lyons previously assaulted. On March 13, 2025, Lyons assaulted a 16-year-old at a Wawa gas station in Port Charlotte, sucker-punching the teenager in the side of the face as he held a door open. Following the arrest, the 20th Judicial Circuit court system placed Lyons into a specialized Mental Health Court diversion program. VIOLENT TRANSIT ATTACKS IN ATLANTA, NEW YORK AND CHARLOTTE FUEL CALLS FOR TOUGHER TRACKING OF REPEAT OFFENDERS The teen’s mother, Shawna Gentry, told Fox News Digital that she fought the diversion track, asking the state prosecutor to seek jail time, alcohol classes and probation. She said she warned judicial officials at the time that Lyons was an active, volatile threat. Charlotte County court minutes show the court terminated Lyons’ probation on July 6, with no objection from the State Attorney’s Office. The minutes included the handwritten words: "Graduation! Congratulations!" alongside a hand-drawn smiley face. VIRGINIA MAN ACQUITTED BY INSANITY IN KILLING FLEES US DURING 48-HOUR MENTAL HOSPITAL PASS "The way the court handled it, the way the state attorney handled it was very odd to me," Gentry said. "They told us they were sending him to a mental health facility, but he never went to a secured place. From what we saw, they just put him right back onto outpatient probation in our neighborhood and cut us completely out of the process." Gentry also challenged the narrative that Lyons suffered a psychiatric break during his attacks. She felt Lyons weaponized mental health language as a calculated legal shield. FLORIDA AG SEEKS JUDGE'S IMPEACHMENT AFTER BABY DROWNING COVID INSANITY ACQUITTAL "When the sheriff came, it was almost like he knew exactly what to say," Gentry said. "He immediately said, 'Well, I've got mental health issues.' He was so quick to use that word." She also said that Lyons appeared visibly intoxicated during the 2025 assault. CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND The court provided no tracking updates, safety alerts, or transitional monitoring to his prior victims, Gentry said. Months later, Lyons walked into the Punta Gorda Publix. Mental health courts The National Treatment Court Resource Center counted 679 adult mental health courts nationwide at the end of 2024. A 2021 analysis of 30 evaluations linked mental health court participation to 74% lower odds of repeat offending. Research on offenders with mental disorders suggests that recidivism depends more on criminal history than on diagnosis. A 2005 study published in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence found that the number of previous offenses was the strongest predictor of reoffending. "Big old tears welled up in his eyes and he said, 'Mom, the guy that hit me just stabbed an old man at Publix. You were right.'" GOT A TIP? articles.title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
articles.summary: The Princess of Wales launches a project encouraging a greater emphasis on children learning from nature.
articles.body:
The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development.

"Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.

This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.

She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".

In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".

She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons .

This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.

She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.

A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project.

"This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess.

"We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing.

"My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."

Catherine has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.

There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".

The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

articles.title: Indian police detain ‘cockroach’ movement founder Dipke ahead of protest
articles.summary: Police detained India‘s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India‘s election chief.
articles.body: Police detained India‘s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India‘s election chief. The youth-led ‘Cockroach Janta Party’ (CJP), opposition groups, and student organizations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favoring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban. The group and left-wing student organizations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag. The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away. “We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke. “I have not broken any law right now...how can you detain me,” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away. There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention. Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest.

articles.title: First images of pope released since lung surgery as Leo celebrates mass in makeshift chapel
articles.summary: The first images of Pope Leo since his lung cancer surgery have been released, showing him standing up and celebrating mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
articles.body: The first images of Pope Leo since his lung cancer surgery have been released, showing him standing up and celebrating mass in a makeshift hospital chapel. Leo led mass at midday on Friday with off-duty medical and nursing staff from the Gemelli Hospital present as the Vatican said he showed “steady improvement” after having part of his lung removed earlier in the week. The pope thanked staff for their work caring for himself and others who are sick during his homily, the Vatican said. The Mass took place in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where a suite of rooms is set aside for any time a pope is admitted for medical treatment. The Vatican also said that Pope Leo will recite the traditional Angelus prayers on Sunday in what will be his first public appearance since his treatment. In the latest update from the Vatican, the press office said Leo underwent blood tests and a chest X-ray on Friday morning. The pontiff is continuing his respiratory physiotherapy sessions, doctors involved in his treatment said, adding that his recovery allows him to carry out normal daily activities independently. The 71-year-old is completely autonomous now in movement and breathing, the Vatican added. Post-operative test results to confirm whether the pope is completely cancer free and what, if any, treatment is needed have not been released yet. The news of the pope’s diagnosis has been received with shock inside the Vatican, with Leo known as someone as physically active and seen to be in good health. The pope’s engagements have been cancelled until 20 October and it is not clear whether his planned trip to Latin America from 6-17 November will take place. The Vatican, however, are continuing with preparations for the visit and on Friday posted the list of journalists traveling with the pope to report on the trip. This story has been updated.

articles.title: US senators call for investigation into Ukraine Starlink restrictions
articles.summary: Ukraine says temporary speed limits to the Starlink internet network disrupted its battlefield missions.
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into reported disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection.

In the letter, sent on Thursday to the US Department of Defense inspector general, the senators say they have "grave concern" about reports of speed restrictions between 12 and 14 October.

The White House and Pentagon have not responded to the suggestion the US might have had a role in the alleged slowdown.

The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors.

It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure".

Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.

The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine.

"We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says.

"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add.

The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats.

Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

SpaceX owner Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind restrictions.

On Wednesday Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".

Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is designed for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk's SpaceX.

Ukraine's President Zelensky has accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites.

On Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine's attacks would continue after Russia had continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure during an "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday.

Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days and would agree to the "energy ceasefire" if Moscow also abided by it. However, he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced.

The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal and Russia said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied.

Zelensky has also criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

articles.title: Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
articles.summary: Families demand justice for the 35 people killed; relatives say they had warned that the roof was leaking.
articles.body:
Authorities in Pakistan have ordered inspections of regional schools after the collapse of a classroom roof killed at least 34 children and a teacher.

Reports on Friday said that the government has ordered the administration of the northeastern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to launch the checks after the deadly incident at Al-Khair school on Thursday.

At least 34 students aged 13 or younger, as well as a teacher, were killed in the roof collapse.

There are conflicting reports about whether the inspections will cover both public and private schools or only private schools. The province’s education department has been given three days to report its findings, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Schools are to be classified as safe, in need of repairs or improvements, or potentially unsafe. Various structures will be assessed, including roofs, ceilings, walls and staircases.

Police arrested Mohammad Khan, the owner of Al-Khair school, shortly after the roof of mud and bricks collapsed.

The building was structurally weak, according to Peshawar Police Chief Saeed Ahmed, who also said that Khan had told officers that recent rains had weakened the structure.

Bereaved families are demanding justice, with some of the victims’ relatives maintaining that they had warned Khan about rainwater repeatedly seeping into classrooms.

Dozens of mourners gathered outside the school on Friday to remember those who died.

Pakistan’s construction standards are widely reported to be poor and builders commonly use substandard materials.

The roof of a private tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore collapsed in June , killing 14 people.
